answer:
The assigned source gives x(n)=nL for integer n>=0 and identifies L as a length scale. It assigns no time map t(n) and no clock interval. Those facts determine the spatial difference x(n+1)-x(n)=L. The index counts positions; no elapsed time or time unit is assigned to its increment. A length per index step therefore does not determine a speed, which has units of length/time. Neither a propagation speed nor its identification with c follows from this source alone.

An additional proposed assumption is the uniform clock t(n)=n tau, where tau is a finite positive interval with units of time. This clock is not an assigned source fact. Conditional on that proposal, for integers m>n>=0, the interval velocity is [x(m)-x(n)]/[t(m)-t(n)]=(m-n)L/[(m-n)tau]=L/tau. Its magnitude, the interval speed, is |L|/tau. If the positive-length convention L>0 is also adopted, the speed is L/tau. Length in metres and tau in seconds would yield metres/second. Using positive-duration intervals avoids the undefined expression x(0)/t(0). These ratios concern sampled events; instantaneous velocity and motion between them require further trajectory or interpolation assumptions.

The proposed clock is not uniquely selected by the positions. Tau and 2 tau preserve every assigned x(n) while giving different interval velocities, L/tau and L/(2 tau). For proposed L>0, any proposed positive speed V can be reproduced by choosing tau=L/V. A different proposed clock, t(n)=n^2 tau, is strictly increasing on the assigned nonnegative integer domain and gives consecutive-step velocity L/[(2n+1)tau]. It therefore permits variable step velocities for the same positions. These counterexamples establish lack of identifiability; neither clock has been established as a physical description.

Finite tau>0 ensures a nonzero elapsed interval in the uniform proposal. For fixed proposed L>0, L/tau grows without bound as tau approaches zero from above and approaches zero as tau approaches infinity; tau=0 itself supplies no defined interval speed. These are algebraic limits, with no physical permission or propagation bound implied. If L=0, the sampled interval displacement is zero for a positive elapsed interval, while motion between sampled events remains undetermined. The source domain supplies no negative-index behavior.

Identifying the conditional speed with c requires stating what c denotes. A model definition c:=|L|/tau, or c:=L/tau under the proposed positive-length convention, permits that notation but supplies no independently determined numerical value or physical law. If c denotes an independently defined physical propagation constant, the identification needs a justified time relation for these events, the length scale and units, an operational definition of what propagates and which intervals and regime are measured, and independent justification or measurement linking the interval speed to that constant. Setting tau=L/c for positive L and c imports the desired value and then reproduces it; it does not derive c. This answer uses only the packet, algebra and dimensional reasoning and makes no validated physics or Aether-Flow result claim.
